title: Translucency: why great teeth let light in
dek: Natural teeth are slightly see-through at the edges, and veneers that block all light are the fastest way to spot cosmetic work.

body.p: Real teeth are not solid white blocks. Light passes partway into them, bounces around and comes back out. That quality is translucency, and it is one of the main reasons a natural smile looks alive. When a restoration lacks it, the teeth can look painted on, even if the color is close.

A tooth is built in layers. Dentin, the inner layer, carries most of the color. Enamel, the outer shell, is more glass-like and lets more light through. Research on natural incisors shows translucency is highest at the biting edge, where enamel is thin and there is little dentin behind it, and it drops steadily toward the gumline. That gradient is why the tips of healthy front teeth can look faintly blue-gray or clear while the middle looks warmer and more solid.

Dental researchers treat natural enamel as the reference that tooth-colored materials should be measured against. Translucency affects how deep a color looks and how well a restoration blends with the teeth beside it.

ul: Excellent: the edges have a soft, slightly see-through quality, and the color deepens gradually toward the gums.
Excellent: in bright light the teeth look like they have depth, not a flat surface.
Giveaway: the same dense white from gumline to tip, with no change at the edges.
Giveaway: teeth that look chalky or opaque, almost like porcelain tiles, especially next to natural lower teeth.
Giveaway: the opposite problem, edges so gray or clear that the teeth look thin or worn.

body.p: Translucency is a balance. Too little looks fake. Too much can look dull or dark, particularly if the tooth underneath is discolored and the material has to hide it. Good work manages that trade-off on purpose.

ul: Look at the biting edges of the upper front teeth in daylight from a window. You want a subtle shift in tone, not a hard line.
Compare upper and lower teeth in a photo. If the uppers look like a different material entirely, translucency is often the reason.
Check a photo taken with flash. Very opaque veneers tend to flare into a flat white in flash photos.
Look from slightly above and to the side. Natural depth shows from angles, not only straight on.

body.p: At a consultation, ask how the dentist and lab plan to handle translucency for your teeth, especially if your natural teeth are darker and need masking. Ask to see before-and-after photos taken in natural light and up close, not only polished studio shots. The answer depends on your own teeth, so an in-person exam is where the real plan gets made.

title: Tooth anatomy: every tooth has a job and a shape to match
dek: Natural front teeth each have their own shape, ridges and contours, so identical rectangles in a row are a clear sign of cookie-cutter work.

body.p: Look closely at an unrestored smile and no two teeth are quite alike. The two front teeth are the largest and most dominant. The ones beside them are smaller and softer. The canines are stronger, with a point. That variety is tooth anatomy, and good cosmetic dentistry respects it. Poor work flattens it into a row of matching tiles.

Each front tooth has an outline, a front surface that curves, and edges that round into the sides. Central incisors are broad and fairly square at the corners. Lateral incisors are narrower, with more rounded corners and slightly shorter edges. Canines have a central ridge and a tip, and they turn the corner of the smile toward the back teeth. Smile-design literature treats these individual tooth characteristics as part of the analysis, alongside the midline, the lip line and the space at the corners of the mouth.

Planning tools reflect this. Careful veneer cases typically start with a diagnostic wax-up or digital design that shapes each tooth individually, then a mock-up that lets the patient see the shapes before any tooth is prepared.

ul: Excellent: centrals, laterals and canines are clearly different shapes that still look related.
Excellent: the front surface has gentle curves and highlights, so light catches each tooth a little differently.
Giveaway: every tooth is the same width and shape, like a strip of identical rectangles.
Giveaway: canines that have been squared off and look like extra front teeth.
Giveaway: flat front surfaces that reflect light as one big shine.
In a straight-on photo, cover all but one tooth on each side. Do the centrals, laterals and canines each have their own character?
Look at the corners of the front teeth. Natural laterals are usually more rounded than centrals.
Turn your head slightly. The canine should lead the eye around the curve of the arch, not face forward like a front tooth.
Look at reflections. Natural anatomy breaks light into soft vertical highlights rather than one flat glare.

body.p: Anatomy is not about making teeth look imperfect. It is about making them look like teeth. At a consultation, ask whether you can preview the planned shapes in a mock-up, and ask how the shapes will be adjusted to your face rather than chosen from a single template. Good cosmetic dentistry does not announce itself, and individual tooth anatomy is a big part of why.

title: Proportion: why size relationships matter more than size
dek: Teeth look natural when their width, length and relationship to each other are in balance, not when they are simply bigger or whiter.

body.p: A smile can be bright, straight and still look wrong. Often the problem is proportion. Teeth that are too wide for their length, front teeth that are not dominant enough, or side teeth that are as large as the centrals all read as artificial. Proportion is about relationships, not a single measurement.

body.h: What proportion means in a smile

body.p: Dentists look at two main relationships. The first is the shape of each tooth: how its width compares with its length. Natural upper central incisors are longer than they are wide, and many smile-design plans aim for a width that is roughly three-quarters to four-fifths of the length. The second is how the teeth relate to each other from the front: the centrals are widest, the laterals are noticeably narrower, and the canines appear narrower still because they turn around the curve of the arch.

You may hear about the golden proportion and similar grids. Smile-design reviews describe them as reference tools, not laws. Faces, lips and arch shapes vary, so the right proportions for one person may not suit another.

ul: Excellent: the two front teeth lead, and the teeth step down in visible width toward the back.
Excellent: teeth look slightly longer than wide, in harmony with the lips and face.
Giveaway: square, short front teeth that look wide and heavy.
Giveaway: laterals almost as wide as centrals, which flattens the smile into a uniform row.
Giveaway: teeth that are oversized for the mouth, pushing the lips forward or filling the smile edge to edge.
In a straight-on photo, compare the two front teeth with their neighbors. The centrals should be clearly dominant.
Look at a single front tooth. If it looks as wide as it is long, it may read as boxy.
Relax your lips. Teeth that look too big often make the lips appear stretched or pushed out.
Compare with older photos. A sudden change in how full your mouth looks can be a proportion issue.

body.p: Proportion often depends on more than the teeth. Gum levels, bite and the space available all shape what is possible, and sometimes gum or orthodontic treatment comes first. At a consultation, ask how the planned proportions were chosen for your face, and ask to preview them in a mock-up before committing. Ask whether your gums need to be part of the plan.

title: Edge design: the line your lower lip should follow
dek: The biting edges of the upper teeth should form a gentle curve that follows the lower lip, and a perfectly flat, straight edge line is a classic giveaway.

body.p: When you smile, the line made by the tips of your upper front teeth is one of the first things people see. In a youthful, natural smile, that line curves gently upward at the sides, following the lower lip. Flatten it into a ruler-straight edge and the smile can look older, artificial or both.

Dentists call the curve of the upper edges the smile arc. Smile-design literature describes the ideal as consonant, meaning the curve of the upper incisal edges runs roughly parallel to the inner curve of the lower lip in a posed smile. A flat smile arc is one where the edges run straighter than the lip. The arc also tends to flatten naturally with age and wear.

Edge design is also about the small details. The two central incisors are usually slightly longer than the laterals. The small V-shaped gaps between tooth tips, called incisal embrasures, are typically narrow at the center and open a little more toward the sides. Edges that are too long or poorly planned can also be more likely to chip if they clash with the bite.

ul: Excellent: the edge line curves gently with the lower lip.
Excellent: centrals sit a touch longer than laterals, with small, natural embrasures between tips.
Giveaway: a perfectly straight line across all the upper teeth, like a cut hedge.
Giveaway: no embrasures at all, so the teeth look fused into one block.
Giveaway: edges that tilt, with one side visibly longer than the other.
Take a straight-on photo of a full, natural smile with the camera level with your mouth. Trace the tips of the upper teeth with your eye and compare with the lower lip.
Look at the tips of the front teeth. Can you see small notches between them, or one continuous edge?
Check symmetry. Draw an imaginary line across the edges. Does it slope to one side?
Say a few words in the mirror. Edges that are too long may touch the lower lip or affect certain sounds.

body.p: Edge position affects looks, speech and bite at the same time, so it is planned in the mouth, not only on a screen. At a consultation, ask whether you can try the planned edge position in a temporary mock-up, and how the dentist will check it against your bite. Your own lip line and bite decide what is right for you.

title: Gum symmetry: the frame most people forget
dek: Even, gently scalloped gums frame a smile, and uneven or puffy gum lines can undermine otherwise good veneers.

body.p: Teeth get the attention, but the gums are the frame. Gum lines that are even, healthy and gently curved make teeth look well proportioned. Gum lines that are uneven, swollen or showing too much can make even beautiful veneers look off. Gum symmetry is often what separates good work from a truly finished result.

body.h: What healthy gum design looks like

body.p: Healthy gums are firm and pink, with a scalloped edge that arches over each tooth. The highest point of each arch is called the gingival zenith. On the front teeth, the gum lines are usually matched from left to right: the two centrals at similar heights, the laterals often sitting slightly lower, and the canines up near the level of the centrals. Small papillae fill the triangles between teeth.

When gum levels are uneven, or teeth look short because gum tissue covers more of them than usual, periodontists can reshape the tissue. The American Academy of Periodontology notes that crown lengthening can be done on one tooth to even the gum line or on several teeth to reveal a broader smile. In some cases this is planned together with veneers so the teeth and the gums are designed as one.

ul: Excellent: gum lines on the left and right match, with a soft arch over each tooth.
Excellent: tissue looks pink and tight around the edges of restorations.
Giveaway: one front tooth with a noticeably higher or lower gum line than its twin.
Giveaway: red, puffy or bleeding gums along the edges of veneers or crowns, which can point to bulky margins or plaque build-up.
Giveaway: dark triangles or a gray line at the gumline next to restorations.
Lift your upper lip gently in a mirror and look at the gum line straight on. Compare each tooth with its partner on the other side.
Take a photo of your widest smile. Notice how much gum shows and whether it is even.
Look at the color of the gums along any veneers or crowns. Healthy tissue should match the gums elsewhere.
Floss. Persistent bleeding around one restoration is worth mentioning to a dentist.

body.p: Gum work is a medical decision, not just a cosmetic one, and the cause of uneven gums matters. At a consultation, ask whether your gum levels were evaluated as part of the plan, whether a periodontist should be involved and what the options are. An in-person exam is needed to tell what is driving your gum line.

title: Shade matching: white is a color, natural is a design decision
dek: Good shade matching blends restorations with the teeth around them and with your face, while a shade that is too white or too flat stands out instantly.

body.p: White is a color. Natural is a design decision. The shade of a veneer or bonding is not just how light it is. It is how well it sits beside your other teeth, your skin and your eyes, in daylight and indoor light. When shade matching goes wrong, it is often the first thing strangers notice.

Tooth color is usually described in three parts. Value is how light or dark the tooth is. Chroma is how intense the color is. Hue is the color family, such as more yellow or more red. Shade-selection reviews describe a common order: judge value first, then chroma, then hue. Value matters most because the eye notices lightness differences quickly.

Shade is also affected by the conditions it is chosen in. Guidance in the dental literature includes using balanced daylight or color-corrected light, avoiding bright surroundings, removing lipstick, and taking the shade while teeth are still moist, because dried teeth look lighter. Dentists use shade guides, and many also use digital tools. The review concludes that combining visual and instrumental methods is a sensible approach.

ul: Excellent: restorations blend with neighboring natural teeth, including the lower teeth.
Excellent: the white looks bright but believable for your skin tone and age.
Giveaway: veneers on the upper teeth that are far whiter than untouched lower teeth.
Giveaway: one crown or veneer that is a slightly different color from the rest.
Giveaway: a flat, uniform white with no variation from gumline to edge.
Look in a mirror by a window during the day, not only under bathroom lights.
Compare the upper front teeth with the lower front teeth and the side teeth.
Check photos in different lighting: daylight, indoor and flash. A good match holds up in all three.
Look for any single tooth that seems a different color from its neighbors.

body.p: Timing matters too. The ADA notes that whitening does not work on veneers, crowns or fillings, so if you plan to whiten, it usually makes sense to do it before restorations are matched. At a consultation, ask how the shade will be chosen, in what light, and whether you will see it in your mouth before it is finalized.

sources.title: Shade Selection in Esthetic Dentistry: A Review — Cureus (PMC)

title: Surface texture: the detail you feel before you see
dek: Natural enamel has fine ridges and a soft sheen, and restorations that are glassy-smooth or dull stand out even when the color is right.

body.p: Color gets most of the attention, but texture decides how teeth catch the light. Natural enamel is not perfectly smooth. It has fine ridges, gentle grooves and a soft sheen. A restoration that is too glassy, too dull or too uniform can look wrong even when the shade is right.

Healthy enamel carries tiny horizontal growth lines called perikymata, along with broader vertical ridges and shallow grooves on the front surface. Research on enamel surfaces shows these ridges are clearly visible on sound teeth and tend to smooth away with wear and erosion. That is one reason younger teeth often look more textured and older teeth more polished.

Gloss is the other half. A study of composite materials notes that the human eye can easily detect differences in gloss even when colors match, and that gloss depends on surface roughness. The same study found the shine of polished composite can fade over time, especially with acidic drinks. Matching texture and keeping it maintained are both part of good work.

ul: Excellent: soft, broken highlights across each tooth, similar to the natural teeth nearby.
Excellent: a sheen that looks like healthy enamel, neither mirror-like nor matte.
Giveaway: one bright, uniform reflection across the whole front of a tooth, like glass.
Giveaway: bonded teeth that have gone dull or rough compared with their neighbors.
Giveaway: upper veneers with a completely different shine from untreated lower teeth.
Stand near a window and tilt your head slowly. Watch how the light moves across the front teeth. Natural texture breaks it into small highlights.
Zoom into a close-up photo. Look for faint lines or ridges on natural teeth and compare with any restorations.
Run your tongue over the front surfaces. Bonding that feels rough or catches may need polishing.
Compare restored and natural teeth side by side in the same light.

body.p: Texture is planned by the dentist and the ceramist, and it should suit your age and your other teeth. At a consultation, ask how surface texture and shine will be matched to your natural teeth, and how restorations should be cared for and polished at checkups. Your dentist can tell you what level of texture fits your smile.
